meta.location: The court and prison of king Noah, in the land of Lehi-Nephi

world_behind.title: A city with no exit and no appeal
world_behind.text: Zeniff's colony sits inside Lamanite territory, and Noah's own watchtower was built high enough to overlook the land the Lamanites hold. There is no higher court than the king and no safe country outside the walls. When Alma runs in verse 3, he is running into the only wilderness available, and the king's servants are sent after him into it.

world_behind.title: A court with no independent accuser
world_behind.text: The king commands, the priests advise, and the men who supply the accusation are the same men who lost the argument in the four preceding chapters. No one in the room appears to have an interest in the outcome that differs from anyone else's, which is why the charge can be swapped at verse 12 without anyone objecting.

world_behind.title: Death by fire, and what it was for
world_behind.text: Burning was reserved in Israel's law for a narrow set of offences and worked as erasure. A body that is burned is not buried and leaves nothing to visit. Abinadi's answer is to name what the fire will not reach: his words will stand.

world_behind.title: Three days in a cell
world_behind.text: The sentence is given in verse 1 and the charge in verse 7, with imprisonment and a consultation between them. The record notes that Noah "counseled with his priests" during the gap and does not say what was decided. What emerges is a charge phrased as a quotation.

world_behind.title: A young man from the right family
world_behind.text: Alma is introduced as a descendant of Nephi, which in this colony is the lineage that confers standing, and he is one of Noah's own priests. The one man who believed was the man with the most to lose by it.

world_behind.title: Writing while hunted
world_behind.text: Verse 4 says he was concealed for many days and wrote all the words Abinadi had spoken. The record does not say what he wrote on or how he remembered it. What it does say is that the writing happened during the hiding.

words.text: Angry, in the older and heavier sense of a settled fury rather than a flash of temper. Treated at Mosiah 10:14. The record uses the comparative in saying the king was "more wroth" and so measures the anger against the plea that caused it. Alma had asked for mercy, and the request made things worse.

Hidden by someone, as opposed to merely out of sight. The verse pairs it with "hid himself," so the same act is described twice, and the second description is the passive one. What he did while concealed is the only thing the verse reports him doing.

A formal charge, the thing a court must produce before it can act. Noah says "we have found an accusation against thee," which admits that it had to be looked for. The verb matters: an accusation that is found rather than brought.

To take back, to withdraw words already spoken. It appears three times in three verses here, more than in the rest of this record put together. The whole negotiation runs on it: Noah offers life for a withdrawal, and Abinadi twice declines in the same word the king used.

Bundles of sticks bound together for burning. It occurs once in scripture, here. The verse says they scourged his skin with them, which makes the fire an instrument of beating before it is a means of death.

Closed and authenticated, the way a document is made binding. The record says he sealed the truth of his words by his death, which treats the death as the final act of the testimony. Nothing is added to the words; they are only made unalterable.

phrases.term: He believed the words which Abinadi had spoken
phrases.text: The narrative turn of the entire unit, stated without emphasis. It is followed immediately by the reason: he knew concerning the iniquity Abinadi had testified against them. That makes the belief a matter of recognizing something already known rather than accepting something new.

phrases.term: Thou hast said that God himself should come down among the children of men
phrases.text: The charge, quoted back almost exactly as Abinadi had said it two chapters earlier (Mosiah 15:1). Noah does not misrepresent him. The accusation is a direct citation. The court understood the sermon and convicted him on the strength of understanding it.

phrases.term: I have suffered myself that I have fallen into your hands
phrases.text: An odd construction that puts the arrest on the prisoner's side of the ledger. He had told them earlier that God would not permit his destruction until he had finished. Now that he has finished, the capture is described as something he allowed, offered as evidence that he believes his own message.

phrases.term: This shall also stand as a testimony against you at the last day
phrases.text: Two things are said to stand: the words, and the innocent blood. Both are described as evidence. Alma's own son will say almost this sentence, watching believers burn at Ammonihah decades later (Alma 14:11).

The reason the king nearly let him go, and the record states it as fear of a word rather than fear of a man. Noah is not persuaded and not repentant. He is worried about consequences, which turns out not to be enough.

The charge that actually works, and it is not the one in verse 8. The priests drop the theological accusation and substitute an insult to the ruler, and the king who had been about to release a heretic delivers up a critic. The phrase occurs once in scripture.

phrases.term: Even as a wild flock is driven by wild and ferocious beasts
phrases.text: Shepherd imagery run backwards. Everywhere else in this record the flock has a keeper; here it has none, and the ones being scattered are the priests who were supposed to be keeping one. The phrase occurs once in scripture.

Four words, and they are the last thing he says. Stephen says almost the same thing under stones, and adds a plea for his killers. Abinadi does not. The sentence immediately before it is about vengeance, and he leaves that where it is.

verses.label: v. 7–8
verses.title: One proposition, and it is enough to hang a man
verses.text: The record gives the accusation in the king's own words and then gives the ground: "Abinadi, we have found an accusation against thee, and thou art worthy of death. For thou hast said that God himself should come down among the children of men; and now, for this cause thou shalt be put to death." The offence is a single proposition, stated in eleven words, and the record makes no attempt to add other counts to it.

verses.label: v. 13
verses.title: The method reported, with an instrument named
verses.text: The record describes the execution with a specific instrument and no elaboration: "they took him and bound him, and scourged his skin with faggots, yea, even unto death." Faggots are bundles of sticks, so the account is of burning applied by scourging rather than of a pyre. The record spends more words on the last speech than on the killing, and gives the killing no adjective at all.

verses.label: v. 19–20
verses.title: Six words of prayer, and the record's own summary
verses.text: The speech ends on a sentence with no accusation in it: "Thus God executeth vengeance upon those that destroy his people. O God, receive my soul." The record then closes the chapter with its own account of the cause of death, and the cause it names is a refusal, not a doctrine: "having been put to death because he would not deny the commandments of God, having sealed the truth of his words by his death."

chapter.title: The verdict precedes the accusation
chapter.text: Verse 1 has the order for execution; verse 7 has the charge. Between them sit three days of consultation among the priests, which suggests the grounds were assembled afterward.

chapter.title: The charge that kills him is not the charge they found
chapter.text: Verse 8 is doctrinal and Noah was ready to drop it. Verse 12 is political (he has reviled the king) and it works within a single verse. A court that could not convict on the sermon convicted on the insult.

chapter.title: Two versions of what he died for
chapter.text: Noah states the charge as saying God himself should come down among men. Limhi, telling the story to Ammon two generations later, gives a longer version about Christ being the Father and man being made in God's image. Both are things Abinadi actually said; the record preserves the two summaries side by side and never harmonizes them.

chapter.title: The word "recall" carries the whole exchange
chapter.text: Noah uses it once and Abinadi twice, in three consecutive verses. The other two times this book uses it, a king is worrying that his son might take his words back and a captain refuses to take back the terms he has offered. The offer and the refusal are conducted in one shared term, and the disagreement is unusually clean.

chapter.title: Everything upstream depends on verse 4
chapter.text: A hunted man hiding for many days writes down a sermon he heard once. Mosiah 12 through 16 exists because of that sentence, and the record mentions it in passing, between an escape and an arrest.

chapter.title: The prophecy is closed out explicitly, much later
chapter.text: The prophecy at verses 15 through 18 is closed out at Alma 25:9–12, seventy years and eight chapters later, and the audit is itemized: "the words of Abinadi were brought to pass," the seed of the priests identified, "Abinadi was the first that suffered death by fire," and the meaning restated, "this is what he meant." The record even supplies the verifying quotation, "What ye shall do unto me shall be a type of things to come." Few prophecies in these books are checked off that explicitly.

chapter.title: The scene repeats in the next generation
chapter.text: Verse 10 has Abinadi say "if ye slay me ye will shed innocent blood, and this shall also stand as a testimony against you at the last day." At Alma 14:11 the son of the scribe who preserved this sermon stands at another burning and says the same thing, that the Lord receives them "in glory" and that the blood of the innocent "shall stand as a witness against them" at the last day. Mosiah 17:4 records the scribe hiding and writing; the sentence he wrote down is spoken by his son roughly a century later.

chapter.title: Role in the unit
chapter.text: The trial runs Mosiah 11 through 17: the king, the charge, the law, Isaiah, the exposition, the closing argument, and the fire. This chapter ends the prophet's part and begins Alma's, and Mosiah 18:1 opens with Alma teaching the words of Abinadi to people who never heard them.

applications.title: Watch for the charge that gets substituted
applications.text: The objection stated first is often not the one that decides the outcome. When a disagreement suddenly resolves, check whether the grounds changed on the way.

applications.title: Write it down now
applications.text: A man being hunted spent his hiding time copying out somebody else's words. If something has landed on you, the cheapest thing you can do is record it before the details go.

applications.title: Notice the difference between fear and repentance
applications.text: Noah feared the judgments and was still the man who ordered the fire. Being worried about consequences can feel a great deal like having changed your mind.

applications.title: Understood is not the same as winning
applications.text: The court quoted him accurately and killed him for it. Sometimes the problem is not that they missed the point.

applications.title: Ask what would still stand
applications.text: He named two things the fire could not reach. In a situation you may lose, it is worth identifying early which parts of it are not in play.

applications.title: Recognizing beats being convinced
applications.text: Alma believed because he already knew about the iniquity being described. When something persuades you fast, it is often because it named a thing you had been declining to name.

applications.title: Leave the vengeance where it goes
applications.text: His second-to-last sentence assigns the settling to God, and his last one is about his own soul. Handing a grievance over is a way of stopping carrying it.

questions.text: What have I heard that I ought to write down before I lose the shape of it?
Which of my convictions could be quoted back at me accurately and still be worth holding?
Where have I described something that happened to me as something I allowed?
Am I afraid of a consequence, or have I actually changed my mind?
When have I switched to an easier objection because the real one was not working?
What would it mean for my life to authenticate what I have said rather than interrupt it?
